title: Abraham Lincoln and the Sleeping Sentry: Mercy as the Highest Form of Justice
summary: During the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln personally pardoned William Scott, a young Vermont private sentenced to be executed for falling asleep on sentry duty after taking another comrade's shift.
keywords: Abraham Lincoln and the Accusation of Being Two-Faced
full_text:
In September 1861, amidst the opening months of the American Civil War, Private William Scott of the 3rd Vermont Infantry was court-martialed and sentenced to be shot by a firing squad for falling asleep on guard duty.

Scott had not fallen asleep out of negligence. The previous night, he had volunteered to take the guard shift of a sick comrade, enduring nearly forty-eight hours of continuous wakefulness before exhaustion overcame his nineteen-year-old body. Under strict military discipline, however, sleeping on sentry was a capital offense.

Hearing the plea of Scott’s regiment, President Abraham Lincoln rode by carriage to the Chain Bridge military camp in Virginia.

Entering the young soldier's tent, Lincoln sat on a camp stool, took the boy’s trembling hands, and spoke with fatherly gentleness:
"My boy, you were sentenced to be executed tomorrow morning. But I have examined your record, and I know why you fell asleep—you risked your own health to shield a sick comrade. I am going to tear up this death warrant and send you back to your regiment.

However, you must pay me a very heavy bill for this pardon!"

Scott stammered in fear, saying his impoverished farmer parents could mortgage their homestead to raise a few hundred dollars.

Lincoln smiled, his deeply lined face glowing with warm affection:
"No, my friend, your farm is safe. Money cannot buy this bill. There is only one currency that can pay for this pardon:
You must promise me that from this hour onward, you will stand as a brave, honest, and steadfast soldier of the United States. You must promise that you will do your duty faithfully until the day comes when you have paid every debt to your country!"

Weeping with gratitude, Scott swore the oath. Seven months later, at the Battle of Lee's Mills, Scott repeatedly dashed across a river under heavy Confederate fire to carry wounded comrades to safety until he was mortally wounded. As he breathed his last, Scott smiled: "Tell President Lincoln I kept my promise."

Lincoln proved that mercy is not a weakness of the law, but the supreme fulfillment of true justice.
